newsitem.title: CAMEROON: U.N. begins bid to end Nigeria-Cameroon dispute.
newsitem.headline: U.N. begins bid to end Nigeria-Cameroon dispute.

text.p: The United Nations on Monday begins the most serious on-the-spot bid yet to end a border row that has brought Nigeria and Cameroon to the brink of war.
A U.N. team is due to meet Cameroon President Paul Biya on Monday at the start of an assessment mission into the dispute over the Bakassi peninsula in the oil-rich Gulf of Guinea.
Radio Cameroon said the mission, headed by a special representative of U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, arrived in Yaounde on Saturday.
After talks with Biya, the team will visit Bakassi, a string of impoverished islands in the Gulf of Guinea, before flying to the Nigerian capital Abuja, the radio said.

Nigerian and Cameroonian troops have clashed over the Bakassi peninsula since February 1994 and the two countries accuse each other of massing forces in the area. The most recent clashes in April caused casualties on both sides.
The dispute centres on agreements between former British and German colonisers.
Prior to the U.N. initiative, Nigeria had always maintained that the dispute should be settled within the Lake Chad Commission which links Nigeria with Chad and Cameroon.
Cameroon took the case to the International Court of Justice at the Hague in 1994 but its ruling in March forbidding further fighting did not prevent clashes a month later.
Military sources say both sides wanted to maintain a strong position on the ground to help their claims in the final verdict of the World Court.
Boutros-Ghali proposed sending a fact-finding mission after the April clashes. Both sides accepted the offer but setbacks in diplomatic moves elsewhere delayed the mission, diplomats said.
Talks in Togo aimed at setting up a meeting between presidents of Nigeria and Cameroon were abruptly cancelled in June. Nigeria said Cameroon requested the cancellation.
Togolese President Gnassingbe Eyadema, one of Africa's longest serving heads of state, has been mediating in the dispute on behalf of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU).
The visit of the U.N. mission followed official Nigerian media reports saying both sides were ready to cooperate.
"Now we have both Cameroon and Nigeria which have agreed to cooperate," Nigerian state radio quoted a U.N. spokeswoman in New York as saying last month.
